newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cardoso gets second term boost in Brazil elections.
newsitem.headline: Cardoso gets second term boost in Brazil elections.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's dream of becoming Brazil's first re-elected leader emerged intact from Thursday's municipal elections, despite the drubbing of a right-hand man, analysts said.
"This election is all about continuity and that is good news for the president," said political scientist Walder de Goes.
About 100 million Brazilians, from huge industrial cities to remote villages in the interior, voted for mayors and councillors in elections that came almost halfway into Cardoso's four-year term.

In Sao Paulo, Brazil's biggest city, Cardoso's friend and former planning minister Jose Serra failed to check the presidential ambitions of outgoing mayor Paulo Maluf whose would-be successor, Celso Pitta, fell one percentage point short of the 50 percent he needed to win in the first round.

Maluf was runner-up in Brazil's first presidential elections after the military dictatorship in 1985, when he was supported by the generals, and he is widely expected to use his support in Sao Paulo as a springboard for another shot at the presidency.
Pitta, a previously unknown bureaucrat, now faces a Nov. 15 run-off against Luiza Erundina of the left-wing Worker's Party (PT) who pipped Serra to second place.

The PT, whose efficient city halls have made it a force in local politics, performed strongly in Thursday's elections, retaining Porto Alegre in Brazil's south in the first round and getting candidates into several run-offs. Cardoso's Social Democratic Party will be involved in run-offs in Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte, Brazil's third largest city.

Analysts noted that in Sao Paulo, Rio and other cities, candidates representing continuity of the current administrations came out on top. Consultant Paulo Calmon said the desire for more of the same might help Cardoso should he win the chance to stand in the 1998 presidential elections.
"This is a big boost for Cardoso in terms of the re-election amemdment," Calmon said. "I think there's a very good chance we will see the re-election issue settled this year."

With congressmen due back in Brasilia after several weeks' absence for campaigning, the government is expected to push soon for approval of a constitutional amendment that would allow Cardoso, state governors and mayors, to stand for a second term. Brazil's Constitution limits holders of executive office to one term.

To win the three-fifths support the re-election bill needs in both house of Congress, the government will have to weave a web of support among the 16 parties in the volatile Chamber of Deputies, including Maluf's Brazilian Progressive Party.
